transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-30
Time: 10:00 AM PST
Duration: ~35 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Li (Redwood AE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (HorizonPay Head of ML), Lina Park (Infra), Aisha Khan (PM)

Summary: quick sync on the POC throughput results from the last run, tuning knobs we tried (continuous batching, concurrency caps, queueing/backlog), and next steps to validate production canary. Customer wants p95 < 400ms at 2k req/min sustained, and fallback plan for peaks.

Topics: results review; continuous batching heuristics; concurrency targets and queue depth; router/queue behavior under burst; KV cache hit rate; quantization impact; plan for dedicated canary.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Li: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, happy thursday, quick agenda - results from last week's stress run, what we changed (we turned on continuous batching, bumped the max batch size and adjusted queueing), and then plan for an extended run.
[00:18] Carlos Mendes: yeah thanks Jordan, quick context, our traffic pattern is spiky, i mean like 30s bursts where we see a lot of small requests, so batching helps but latency can't blow up, we need p95 under 400ms ideally.
[00:32] Priya Menon: got it, so in the last run we enabled continuous batching in the runtime, set target batch window to 8ms and max batch size 64, also tried aggressive KV cache prefetching. The observed throughput improved about 38% but p95 moved to ~520ms on the heavier tails.
[00:50] Lina Park: just to confirm network wasn't the bottleneck right? our infra team captured the VPC logs, there were a few retransmits but nothing huge, i can upload them.
[01:02] Priya Menon: yeah from Redwood's side CPU/GPU utilization sat at about 92% across the 4 GPUs in the dedicated test pool, so we were compute-bound at peak; continuous batching reduced per-token overhead though.
[01:18] Aisha Khan: can you explain the p95 move up a bit? is that because some requests waited longer while the runtime accumulated bigger batches?
[01:26] Priya Menon: partially, yes. Continuous batching trades a small waiting window for throughput. When traffic is very bursty with many small requests, some requests land in later micro-batches and that increases tail latency. We also saw some queueing at the request router when concurrency hit the cap.
[01:39] Carlos Mendes: what concurrency cap did you use for that run?
[01:42] Priya Menon: we used a concurrency target of 80 in the front router and a per-worker parallelism of 20. We tried a few configs: 80/20 default, 120/30, and a conservative 60/15. The 120/30 pushed throughput highest but tail latency suffered unless we also reduced batch window to 4ms.
[02:00] Jordan Li: note that decreasing the batch window reduces batch sizes and so per-token efficiency drops, so cost goes up. There's a balance point where throughput gains justify the more frequent kernel launches.
[02:12] Lina Park: do you have the numbers for cost delta when moving window from 8ms to 4ms?
[02:16] Jordan Li: rough ballpark from the test infra: 8ms -> baseline unit cost, 4ms increased unit cost by about 18-22% due to smaller batches and more kernel overhead. We'll include exact spreadsheet.
[02:30] Priya Menon: also worth calling out quantization profile — we tested 4-bit quant with A-quant mix, it shaved latency by ~12% p50 but had mixed effects on p99 for some seq lengths; quality was okay on our eval prompts but we flagged two prompt patterns that slightly hallucinated.
[02:48] Carlos Mendes: not great for financial phrasing, we need to preserve fidelity on numbers. That might block rolling 4-bit broadly.
[02:55] Aisha Khan: could we scope quantization just for non-sensitive routes? like embeddings / internal tools?
[03:00] Priya Menon: yes that's a common pattern, route-level quantization. Redwood can route different endpoints to different model variants or quant profiles — the runtime supports automatic fallback.
[03:12] Jordan Li: returning to throughput: one thing we tested was queueing behavior, we added a small request queue with token-level prefilling to let the runtime shape batches better, this added about 6-8ms mean delay but reduced p95 in some configs because it avoided huge variance in batch sizes.
[03:28] Lina Park: so queue adds fixed delay but improves tail, interesting. Any risk of queue growing unbounded under sustained spikes?
[03:35] Priya Menon: the router has backpressure and an admission control; we configured max queue depth to 500 requests for the test and a soft drop policy. In practice once the queue hits threshold we start shedding low-priority traffic or route to a lower-cost region.
[03:50] Carlos Mendes: shedding low-priority is ok, we have a small % of non-critical inference. For payments though, we need strict SLOs. Could we pin those routes to dedicated capacity?
[03:58] Jordan Li: absolutely, that's the recommended pattern — critical payment routes on Dedicated pool with higher concurrency cap and reserved GPU ratio. Less critical routes go to hosted pool or cheaper quantized variants.
[04:10] Aisha Khan: when we say "reserved GPU ratio" what's the typical headroom you recommend for peak 20% bursts?
[04:17] Priya Menon: we generally suggest 30-40% headroom for spiky workloads; plus a burst policy that allows short-term capacity above commit for 60–120s. That can be tuned with autoscale and burst settings.
[04:30] Carlos Mendes: ok what about fallback behavior — if the dedicated pool is saturated do you route to hosted? how does state/consistency work?
[04:38] Jordan Li: Redwood's smart routing can be policy-driven — route by latency or cost, and you can opt for automatic fallback to a compatible model variant in another pool. For stateful session-like flows we recommend sticky routing or KV cache replication; for stateless payment checks, fallback is straightforward.
[04:54] Priya Menon: small note on KV cache: we saw 78% KV hit rate in the last run when we warmed with typical prefixes, that shaved about 9% off token compute. If the cache misses spike during bursts p95 suffers.
[05:07] Lina Park: can we measure prefix distribution? we'll send our production sample.
[05:11] Carlos Mendes: yes we'll share 24h sample and target QPS windows.
[05:15] Jordan Li: perfect. Next, the extended stress plan: Priya will run a 2-hour test with 200 concurrent clients simulating our burst pattern (10s high, 50s low) to see sustained behavior, we'll capture p50/p95/p99 and queue depth over time.
[05:28] Priya Menon: i'll include per-model batch size distribution, queue depth, and GPU kernel times. Also will test a 4ms window vs 8ms and a mid point 6ms to see tradeoffs.
[05:40] Aisha Khan: how do we validate the canary threshold? what metrics do we require to go forward?
[05:44] Jordan Li: propose p95 <= 400ms, p99 <= 800ms during sustained 2k req/min with 30% burst headroom; KV hit >= 70% for cached routes; no more than 1% errors. If those metrics are met we move to a small dedicated canary.
[06:00] Carlos Mendes: sounds reasonable, we'll confirm internally.
[06:04] Priya Menon: one more wrinkle — network MTU and serialization can contribute a few ms if payloads are large. Lina, could you validate that the MTU is standard and no extra proxies are adding latency?
[06:14] Lina Park: yes we have an NLB and an internal proxy, there was a misconfigured timeout in a previous run, i've already adjusted that but will re-check MTU and path.
[06:23] Jordan Li: great, and we'll attach the exact runtime config we used in the run: batch window, max batch size, queue depth, concurrency caps, quant profile. That should make reproducing straightforward.
[06:33] Aisha Khan: what about cost estimation for dedicated vs hosted at the target throughput? can you share that in the spreadsheet?
[06:38] Jordan Li: yes we'll include unit cost numbers for each config we tested and an estimated monthly cost for the target sustained QPS and the assumed 30% headroom.
[06:47] Priya Menon: i'll also include a sensitivity table: cost vs p95 at different batch windows and concurrency caps so you can pick a sweet spot.
[06:56] Carlos Mendes: i heard you mention fallback to quantized variant, does that require any model conversion step that takes time?
[07:02] Priya Menon: we usually pre-compile quantized variants during onboarding; conversion is a one-time job and we can pre-warm them. Runtime switching is near-incidental once variants exist.
[07:12] Aisha Khan: ok good.
[07:14] Jordan Li: last thing — security docs, SOC2, SAML, KMS — i'll attach the certs and the SOC2 report to the follow up.
[07:21] Carlos Mendes: please do, security is the gating factor for us.
[07:24] Jordan Li: noted. any other blockers?
[07:26] Lina Park: no blockers, just need the logs and config so we can align infra settings.
[07:30] Carlos Mendes: one small ask — can Priya include the exact command lines or helm values you used? our infra team prefers exact manifests.
[07:36] Priya Menon: yep will include helm values and runtime flags.
[07:40] Jordan Li: wrap-up: Jordan shares spreadsheet and security docs by monday (2027-01-03), Priya runs the stress test and uploads results (2027-01-05), Lina shares VPC logs (2027-01-04), Carlos shares traffic pattern (2027-01-06). We'll reconvene after results to decide on a dedicated canary date.
[07:58] Aisha Khan: thanks all.
[08:00] Carlos Mendes: thanks Jordan, Priya.
